title: Ohm's Law Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Clocks and Watches with AI
description: Change the voltage and resistance of a simple loop circuit to see Ohm's Law at work: live current and power readouts, moving dots that speed up with current, and a quiz that asks you to calculate the current.

learningObjectives: Apply Ohm's Law (I = V / R) to calculate the current from a voltage and a resistance.
Predict how the current changes when the voltage or the resistance is doubled or halved.
Calculate electric power with P = V × I.
prerequisites: Read the Voltage, Current, and Resistance section of Chapter 2.
Convert amps to milliamps (1 A = 1,000 mA).

accessibility.notes: Screen-reader description provided; all controls are standard HTML elements.

controls.label: Start / Pause
controls.description: Starts or pauses the moving dots. The MicroSim opens paused.

controls.label: Quiz me
controls.description: Picks a new voltage and resistance and hides the current and power.

controls.label: Answer (mA)
controls.description: Your calculated current in milliamps (shown during a quiz).

controls.label: Check
controls.description: Checks your answer and reveals the current.

keyQuestions: What happens to the current when the resistance doubles?
Which setting gives the largest current, and why is that risky?
How much power does 5 V across 100 Ω use?
commonMisconceptions: Thinking current is used up as it goes around the loop. The same current flows everywhere in a single loop.
Thinking more resistance means more current.
Forgetting to convert amps to milliamps (0.010 A is 10 mA).
assessmentOpportunities: Students correctly calculate the current for any voltage and resistance shown.
Students explain that doubling the resistance halves the current and doubling the voltage doubles it.
Students calculate power in milliwatts from voltage and current.
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Parameter exploration with live readouts and a calculation quiz
